title: The Needle Galaxy
caption: The Needle Galaxy, IC 2233, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A thin sliver of light cuts across this Hubble image, tinged bluish along its length. This is IC 2233, a spiral galaxy seen edge-on and one of the flattest galaxies known, like a silver needle in a haystack of space.

Most spirals, including the Milky Way, have three main visible parts. There is a disc containing the spiral arms along with most of the gas and dust, a sparse halo around it, and a central bulge packed with ancient stars. IC 2233 is a super-thin galaxy, at least ten times wider than it is thick, and like almost all such galaxies it has a low brightness and no bulge at all.

The bluish tint along the disc gives away its spiral nature, pointing to hot, bright young stars born from clouds of gas. Unusually, it has no well-defined dust lane, only a few small patches near its middle.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, combining visible and near-infrared exposures. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared light, invisible to the eye, and the galaxy's low brightness makes it hard to see without long exposures.

explore: IC 2233 lies in the constellation Lynx, about 40 million light-years away, and was first found in 1894 by the British astronomer Isaac Roberts.
A version of this image was entered into Hubble's Hidden Treasures image processing competition by Luca Limatola.
alt: A very thin, edge-on spiral galaxy stretched across the frame with a bluish tint along its disc.
